findings.note: ForwardingMonitor reads /proc/net/snmp's Ip: Forwarding COUNTER. The reviewer inferred the code from the module's comments.

findings.note: needs a targeted test: remove the token check and see whether any test goes red

findings.title: The retrain clock is reset to `now()` whenever only the baseline trains — the exact bug the adjacent comment claims was fixed
findings.note: Fixed already, and the fix's docstring describes this exact finding as the prior behaviour. worker.py:224-239 reads the age from the ARTIFACT (_oldest_trained_at), not from process uptime, and returns it as the second element; the warm-start path no longer stamps now().

findings.title: Empty or unjoined diversity/temporal side-tables degrade scoring with no signal — unlike Zeek, which warns
findings.note: CONFIRMED, and the most consequential of the batch so far. Guard counts measured in weirvern/worker.py: `if not zeek_idx` appears once (with a logger.warning naming the cause); `if not div_idx` and `if not tmp_idx` are ZERO. features.py guards with `if diversity:` / `if temporal:`, so an unjoined side-table silently sets log_unique_dst_ports=log1p(0), port_entropy=0.0, connection_density=1.0, activity_regularity=1.0, burstiness=1.0 -- all PLAUSIBLE-LOOKING values, none of them measured, with no log line anywhere. Every score in the sweep is degraded and nothing says so, while the neighbouring Zeek case DOES warn: an operator loses the one signal that would have told them the difference.

findings.title: A failed anomalies query returns 200 with an empty list — the triage view reads a broken query as a quiet network
findings.note: CORRECTED: my first verdict was REFUTED, and that was too quick. The ROUTE does return 503 -- but the function it calls, anomalies_detailed, swallowed every exception into an empty list at DEBUG level, so the route's failure path was unreachable. A broken query therefore produced HTTP 200 with [] and the view rendered its normal empty state. Fixed: the function now raises, the route's 503 path is reachable, and three tests pin it (mutation-tested).

findings.title: Review state silently expires after 72 hours: `review_index` is time-bounded, the anomalies list is not
findings.note: The route's review_index reads a 72h window while anomalies_detailed has NO time bound, so an anomaly older than the window found no index match and was labelled review_state='' -- which the UI renders as 'nobody has reviewed this'. That is a claim about the OPERATOR'S WORK and it can be false. Fixed: review_index now returns its own covered_since and attach_reviews marks an out-of-window row REVIEW_UNAVAILABLE with a reason. Four tests, mutation-tested three ways (no guard / no naive-aware normalisation / everything unknowable).

findings.title: Netflow "Talkers" panel: query failure renders as "No talkers in this window" — `available` is hardcoded true
findings.note: /api/netflow reports available+reason and the front end gates on it; the DOM harness has 28 failure-vs-empty checks.

findings.title: `.env.example` and `SECURITY.md` contradict each other about which ports face the LAN
findings.note: Measured on the live node: ss -lunp shows goflow2 bound on *:2055 and *:6343 -- every interface, because the collector runs with hostNetwork (added deliberately after a real router sent NetFlow to 2055 while the listener was at 32055 and its packets vanished with NOTHING logged). SECURITY.md said those ports 'are cluster-internal and are not reachable from outside', and README.md repeated it in TWO places, one of which claimed an exporter aimed at 2055 'sends its packets nowhere'. All three were wrong, and they were wrong in the SECURITY document, where a reader goes to learn what is exposed. Corrected in all three files, which now name the two controls (firewall to the exporter addresses; WEIRVERN_FLOW_EXPORTER_ALLOW) and say the protocols are unauthenticated. Guarded by tests/test_docs_port_claims.py, which asserts the CLAIM shape against the MANIFEST shape -- mutation-tested three ways, including that it STANDS DOWN if hostNetwork is ever turned off.

findings.title: The manifest reference checker is blind to `configMapKeyRef` — the most common ConfigMap reference form
findings.note: Reproduced by mutation: renaming a configMapKeyRef to a nonexistent name produced 'problems: NONE' from the CI checker, so it would pass a manifest whose pod cannot start (CreateContainerConfigError on the operator's cluster). The tree has 7 configMapKeyRef uses vs 1 secretKeyRef, so the checker examined the rare shape and ignored the common one. Fixed by matching configMap*/secret* by prefix, and pinned by tests/test_ci_manifest_refs.py which extracts the SHIPPING function from the workflow and drives it with fixtures. Mutation-tested: restoring the original lists fails 4 tests; flagging every name field fails 2.

findings.title: Rotation and restart re-ingest everything already read: offsets are filename-keyed and process-local
findings.note: The re-read is real (measured: 155 files / 111 MB per restart, dns alone 37 files/100 MB) but the claimed CONSEQUENCE is wrong. Zeek tables are ReplacingMergeTree ORDER BY (ts, uid) with uid from Zeek's own log line, so a re-read COLLAPSES onto the existing row. Measured on zeek_dns: 53749 rows vs 51322 distinct (ts,uid) keys; 2 MiB on disk for 100 MB of source text. So the cost is startup parsing work, not duplicate ingest or unbounded growth. Re-read is bounded (depth=50 per type per pass, 24h retention). Documented with numbers in ingester.py; offset-safety pinned by 8 tests, mutation-tested 3 ways.

findings.title: The `(empty)` sentinel is still stored literally — including in `ja4`, the exact bug the docstrings claim was fixed
findings.note: CONFIRMED and FIXED (commit 98530ba), reproduced by hand: map_zeek_ssl read every string field with `rec.get(...) or ""`, bypassing zeek_value, so weirvern.zeek_ssl.ja4 stored the literal 7-character `(empty)` -- which uniqExactIf(ja4, ja4 != '') counts as a REAL DISTINCT FINGERPRINT, so the live zeek_ja4_count ML feature reported 1 for a host with no fingerprint. The read layer normalised `-` only. Fixed in BOTH places: tail_zeek_log now normalises both sentinels (the guarantee a mapper cannot bypass -- 79 raw rec.get reads remain across mappers) and the SSL mapper routes its fields through zeek_value. Also found while fixing: tests/test_ja4_fingerprint_integrity.py passed over the live defect.

findings.title: The mapper↔columns↔table arity contract is enforced nowhere, and one failing INSERT permanently blocks every later log type behind a generic handler
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed. Two defects in the Zeek write path. (1) THE MAPPER/COLUMNS CONTRACT WAS ENFORCED NOWHERE AT RUNTIME: the write is positional (`[row.get(c) for c in columns]`), so a column with no value from the mapper becomes None and a mapper key with no column is DROPPED -- neither is an error anywhere. The two tables ARE compared in the test suite, but for the log types those tests enumerate, which is coverage by enumeration that does not survive a new log type or field, and the production path had no check at all. Verified nothing is broken TODAY: 19 registered log types, 18 with column lists, no mapped type missing one, no columns entry without a mapper. (2) THE POISON PILL, which is what makes the first defect dangerous rather than theoretical: an exception from client.insert escaped tail_zeek_log BEFORE state.note_read ran, so the cursor never advanced. MEASURED: pass 1 raised 'DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected column of type String' and state.offset stayed 0; pass 2 re-read from offset 0 and raised AGAIN. So ONE unparseable record ends that log type permanently -- the worker's loop catches, logs and retries the same line forever, with the only symptom a warning that repeats every cycle. FIXED: a mapper/columns check on the first mapped row per file (once per file, not per row, since the pair is static) raising the new IngesterError; and a batch that fails as a whole is retried ROW BY ROW so only the offending rows are lost, with each rejection NAMED (not merely counted) at WARNING. The rejected row is behind the cursor on the next pass, verified. VERIFIED after the fix: all-good -> 3 inserted, cursor advanced; middle rejected -> 2 inserted, cursor advanced, second pass retries NOTHING; all rejected -> 0 inserted, cursor STILL advances. 10 tests, 6 mutations caught. MY OWN MISTAKE FOUND BY MUTATION: the fix originally reported the ATTEMPTED count, so three rows with one rejected logged 'inserted: 3' -- a confident number about a write that did not happen. `_insert_batch` now returns what LANDED. SECOND MISTAKE: adding the check broke an existing test that scanned a fixed 700-character window after `row = mapper(rec)`; my comment pushed `_excluded(row)` to 2472 characters, so the test failed on the code being correct. That test now slices the enclosing FUNCTION and asserts the ordering, and still catches removal of the filter.

findings.title: The siphon overlay never enables siphon mode
findings.note: Verified against the tree: the overlay granted hostNetwork, NET_RAW, NET_ADMIN and the forwarding sysctls, and left SENSOR_MODE='loch'. Effects: weirvern status reads the configured mode, so the loud check for 'a siphon sensor with no live intercept' was skipped by construction; and the Sluice Gate reported DEGRADED on a deployment an operator had explicitly built to enforce. Fixed with a merge patch wired into the overlay; base still defaults to loch. Mutation-tested four ways.

findings.title: The worker liveness probe is green over a dead detection loop
findings.note: CONFIRMED, fixed, and verified firing. The worker's liveness probe imports only `weirvern.config`, so it proves the interpreter works and cannot see a dead detection loop; the main loop catches every exception and sleeps 30s, so a permanently-failing path restarts nothing. Fixed by a new `detect_loop` health probe reading TWO independent per-cycle signals (baseline_history.computed_at, near_misses.replaced_at), either fresh being proof the loop ran. PROVEN TO FIRE against the live cluster: worker scaled to 0 -> overall ok False, ingest_freshness still ok ('newest flow 5m29s ago', data arriving) while detect_loop reported 'last cycle 9m54s ago ... so the loop has stopped'. That is the previously-invisible state: traffic flowing, detection dead.

findings.title: GUI settings writes are silently reverted by the next `kubectl apply -k`
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT against the live cluster, then fixed. The GUI writes settings into `weirvern-env`, the SAME ConfigMap k8s/20-configmap-env.yaml owns, so `kubectl apply -k` restores the manifest's value. Measured end to end: POST /api/settings/apply {DETECT_INTERVAL_S: 240} -> ok:true, applied 240, restarted the worker -> ConfigMap 240; then `kubectl apply -k k8s/` -> ConfigMap 300. The write path worked as designed and reported success honestly; the defect was that nothing recorded the operator's intent, so after a deploy the change was gone untraceably. NOT FIXABLE BY STRENGTHENING THE WRITE -- the field belongs to the manifest and an apply is entitled to reset it; the codebase already made the opposite trade deliberately for the account store (kustomization.yaml ships no manifest for product-written data, so an apply cannot wipe accounts). FIXED BY MAKING THE CONFLICT LEGIBLE: (1) ClusterConfig.apply records every written key in an annotation with value + ISO-8601 timestamp, accumulating across writes and refreshing (not duplicating) a repeated same-value write; (2) new ClusterConfig.settings_drift reports per key the chosen value, when, the current value and whether it was reverted, returned by the settings view. VERIFIED LIVE: view showed reverted:false with current=240 after the GUI write, then after `kubectl apply -k` showed reverted:true, chosen 240, current 300, at 2026-09-23T12:47:14Z -- and the provenance annotation SURVIVED the apply that reverted the value, which is the point, since it is the record of what was lost. The kustomize and kubectl annotations were undisturbed (merge patch). 15 tests, 6 mutations caught including never-report and always-report. TWO OF MY OWN MISTAKES CAUGHT BY MUTATION: the drift logic was first written inline in the request handler with tests reimplementing it, so breaking the view's `reverted` expression left the ENTIRE SUITE GREEN (moved to settings_drift so view and tests share one implementation); and the first version read current values from the rendered settings payload, which is the GUI PROCESS's start-time view -- reporting 'reverted' on a healthy cluster and 'fine' on a reverted one, the warning inverted (now reads the live ConfigMap).

findings.title: The GUI pod's RBAC is node-root by another name
findings.note: CONFIRMED AGAINST A LIVE CLUSTER, then fixed and verified both ways. The GUI's ServiceAccount (weirvern-operator, automounted) had patch/update on the WHOLE `daemonsets` resource. ds/zeek is privileged:true, holds CAP_NET_RAW and mounts hostPaths -- it must, to capture -- so the operator role could rewrite it. Proven with a SERVER-SIDE DRY RUN (fully validated, nothing written): adding a hostPath volume mounting the host root returned 'daemonset.apps/zeek patched'. The ONLY objection was a PodSecurity WARNING: the namespace is labelled pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged (deliberate, the sensor needs the caps), so nothing enforced it. A compromised GUI pod could therefore mount the node filesystem on every node, and the GUI is a NodePort HTTP service with password auth, so that is not hypothetical. FIXED by scoping the write verbs with resourceNames, verified live to work per object (patch daemonsets/zeek -> yes, patch daemonsets/clickhouse -> no). The grant now covers exactly the three workloads the settings path restarts (ds/zeek, deploy/weirvern-worker, deploy/weirvern-gui -- derived from _RESTART_FOR) and `update` is granted nowhere, since a PUT replaces the whole object and could strip a securityContext. VERIFIED LIVE AFTER APPLY: the hostPath dry-run is REFUSED; patch daemonsets/clickhouse, patch deployments/goflow2 and update deployments are all no; and the GUI still functions -- login ok, /api/settings HTTP 200, the settings WRITE returned ok:true and successfully rolled deploy/weirvern-worker (the RBAC-gated action), /api/health HTTP 200. ONE GRANT CANNOT BE NAMED and is documented as such: the Sonar survey Job has a random suffix (weirvern-sonar-<8 hex>), and resourceNames cannot match a name that does not exist yet. 7 tests, 6 mutations caught including the UNION TRAP (a second unscoped rule silently widening a scoped one) and dropping a restart target. TWO OF MY OWN TEST BUGS, both caught by running them: my resourceNames helper required every rule mentioning a resource to be scoped, which failed on the manifest being RIGHT (a nameless get/list rule is correct and expected) -- it now asks per VERB; and I read `create pods/portforward` as removed when can-i simply wants `--subresource=portforward`, which returned yes. NOTE: report body not recoverable (tmp/k9_k8s.md cleaned).

findings.title: Worker restart loses the tail position: flow history is re-read or gapped
findings.note:
CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed. `tail_forever` built its `TailState()` in memory and never persisted it, so the cursor died with the process. Measured with a 6-row JSONL: two passes in ONE process inserted 6 then 0 (correct, the documented fix), and a RESTART with the file unchanged inserted 6 again. The docstring claims this failure mode solved ('re-reading the whole file from offset 0 every pass inserted every row ~12x per minute into flows, corrupting aggregates and baselines') -- the in-process case was fixed and the restart case left open, which is the same corruption at every pod restart, node reboot and image update. FIXED: the cursor is checkpointed beside the file (atomic replace) and reloaded on start, revalidated with the existing content-based `_offset_is_on_boundary` check so a cursor from before a ROTATION is discarded rather than trusted (honouring it would silently skip everything written since -- losing data is worse than duplicating it, because nothing looks wrong afterwards). Added a `stop` flag so the loop can be shut down and tested. 9 tests, 7 mutations caught. NOTE ON THE TESTS: my first version passed with the fix reverted AND with the checkpoint write deleted entirely, because it exercised load/save in isolation and never called `tail_forever` -- the defect was in tail_forever's wiring. Rewritten to run the real loop on a thread.

=== THE FIX WAS INERT IN PRODUCTION UNTIL A SECOND PASS (found by deploying, not by testing) ===
The first fix checkpointed the cursor BESIDE the tailed file. The deployed worker mounts its flow directory READ-ONLY on purpose, so the log showed 'Could not checkpoint the tail cursor for /data/flows.jsonl: [Errno 30] Read-only file system' on every pass and every restart still re-read the whole file. tmp_path is always writable, so no test could see it: the fixture was more permissive than production. FIXED for real: TAIL_STATE_DIR (default /models, the one writable persistent volume) with the filename derived from the tailed path. VERIFIED ON THE LIVE BOX across two consecutive worker restarts: the cursor exists in the persistent volume, offset 1074419 == the file's exact byte size, ZERO 'Could not checkpoint' warnings, and the second restart logged 'Ingested 1 flow records (offset 1072467)' instead of re-reading ~1086. 13 tests, 8 mutations caught. New regression tests CHMOD the fixture directory to 0555 rather than reasoning about permissions.

findings.title: Tail offsets live only in process memory — every worker restart re-ingests the entire flow file (and ~24h of Zeek logs) as duplicates
findings.note: See F011: offsets are memory-only and filename-keyed so a restart does re-read, but the ingest is idempotent (ReplacingMergeTree on a stable Zeek uid) and bounded. Persisting offsets would remove a real startup cost and is worth doing -- it is not the data-integrity problem reported.

findings.title: NetFlow/sFlow intake is unauthenticated UDP on `hostNetwork` with no source restriction anywhere in the bundle
findings.note: Verified in the manifests: the goflow2 collector runs with hostNetwork (to bind 2055/6343 on the node's own interfaces, because an exporter was observed targeting the container port rather than the NodePort and its packets vanished silently), NetFlow carries no authentication or source verification, k8s/70-networkpolicy.yaml deliberately exempts this collector, and goflow2 has no accept-list. So any device that can reach the node can inject flow records attributed to ANY address, feeding the anomaly models and the charts. FIXED with WEIRVERN_FLOW_EXPORTER_ALLOW (off by default, so no exporter is silently dropped on first boot), enforced at the single point every record passes through, plus 'weirvern exporters' so the list can be written from observed fact. Rejected records are counted and logged at WARNING. 11 tests, mutation-tested 4 ways.

findings.title: The `(empty)` sentinel fix is documented as done at the read layer, but the read layer only normalises `-` — `(empty)` still reaches table columns verbatim
findings.note: CONFIRMED and FIXED (commit 98530ba), reproduced by hand: map_zeek_ssl read every string field with `rec.get(...) or ""`, bypassing zeek_value, so weirvern.zeek_ssl.ja4 stored the literal 7-character `(empty)` -- which uniqExactIf(ja4, ja4 != '') counts as a REAL DISTINCT FINGERPRINT, so the live zeek_ja4_count ML feature reported 1 for a host with no fingerprint. The read layer normalised `-` only. Fixed in BOTH places: tail_zeek_log now normalises both sentinels (the guarantee a mapper cannot bypass -- 79 raw rec.get reads remain across mappers) and the SSL mapper routes its fields through zeek_value. Also found while fixing: tests/test_ja4_fingerprint_integrity.py passed over the live defect.

findings.title: Nothing probes whether the detection loop is alive
findings.note: CONFIRMED ON THE LIVE CLUSTER and FIXED (commit 63bdc2d). MEASURED BEFORE: all three aggregation tables held 16,934/16,870 rows with their newest window_start a 5-minute boundary 315s old while raw flows kept arriving (24,411 rows), and the sweep's own query `window_start >= now() - INTERVAL 300 SECOND` matched ZERO rows. /api/health simultaneously reported clickhouse ok, tables ok 9/9, ingest_freshness ok 58s, zeek_freshness ok 59s, models ok, alerts ok -- DETECTION ANALYSED NOTHING WHILE EVERY PROBE READ GREEN, and nothing anywhere reports detection-cycle activity, which is why it went unnoticed. ROOT CAUSE: the MV buckets on toStartOfFiveMinute while the sweep looked back detect_interval_s=300s FROM NOW, so the bucket and the lookback were the SAME DURATION and raced -- a bucket is visible only while T <= B+300, exactly when its flows stop and the next bucket is empty, and with equal durations the phase never drifts so a sweep can sit in the empty case indefinitely. detection_sweep returns [] on no rows. FIXED by deriving the lookback from the bucket (bucket + one cadence) via a named AGG_BUCKET_S that reads the schema. MEASURED AFTER: window 2 rows -> 4 rows, 316 near misses recorded with the newest at 06:45, and per-cycle logs now show "Baselines computed for 97 hosts", "Recorded 3 near miss(es)" and ATT&CK mapping running every sweep.

findings.title: ml_models rows are written for detectors that never trained
findings.note: CONFIRMED against the live cluster. `_record_model_metadata(client, detectors)` is called BEFORE the `if not trained_any:` guard (weirvern/worker.py, cold-start path AND the full-retrain path), and the helper loops every detector inserting metadata regardless of whether its train() returned True. So an untrained detector gets a training-history row, which is what makes the models probe below unable to tell a working pipeline from a dead one.

findings.title: Models probe reports ok on the mere existence of rows — staleness is fetched and ignored
findings.note: CONFIRMED and measured on the live cluster. The probe selects `max(trained_at) AS last_trained` and then never compares it to anything: `ok=True` is driven purely by `mrows` being non-empty, with the detail string '4 detector(s) with training history'. Measured: every detector's last training was 27.2 HOURS old against RETRAIN_EVERY_H=6 -- 4.5x the interval -- and the probe still reported ok=True. The staleness computation that exists (status._staleness) is used only by model_overview, not by this probe. Combined with F023, a detector that NEVER trained also reports healthy.

findings.title: The retrain clock advances when only the adaptive baseline trains
findings.note: Same code, and the OLDEST artifact governs by construction (worker.py:263-267 documents 'the retrain clock must fire when the stalest model is due, so one freshly-trained detector cannot hold a retrain back'). A baseline-only train cannot advance the full-detector clock.

findings.title: cap_mb=0 — documented as "no cap" — deletes every rotated log older than the grace period
findings.note: CONFIRMED, reproduced by running it: five rotated logs, plan_prune(cap_mb=0) returned ALL FIVE as doomed while cap_mb=1000 returned none, and prune(cap_mb=0) deleted all five BEFORE the fix (0 after). WHY IT MATTERS: config.py documents the setting as "0 means no cap and is reported as unset rather than as within budget", and 0 is the DEFAULT for zeek_max_mb, netflow_max_mb and ml_max_mb. plan_prune did cap_bytes = max(0, cap_mb) * 1024 * 1024, turning 0 into a ZERO-BYTE budget, so every file exceeds it and oldest-first removes everything past the grace period. The live cluster is safe (k8s/20-configmap-env.yaml sets 2048/1024/2048), so this bit a deployment running on the defaults -- exactly what defaults are for, with silent log destruction rather than an error as the failure mode. FIXED in three places: plan_prune returns early for cap_mb <= 0 (covering both the whole-directory and the per_type branch, which divides the cap by group count and so had a second path to the same defect), and prune_loop no longer gates on a comparison that reads 0 as a budget. Four mutations caught, including disabling the pruner entirely.

findings.title: The `(empty)` fix the comments describe was only applied to `-`; the named ja4 path still stores it verbatim
findings.note: CONFIRMED and FIXED (commit 98530ba), reproduced by hand: map_zeek_ssl read every string field with `rec.get(...) or ""`, bypassing zeek_value, so weirvern.zeek_ssl.ja4 stored the literal 7-character `(empty)` -- which uniqExactIf(ja4, ja4 != '') counts as a REAL DISTINCT FINGERPRINT, so the live zeek_ja4_count ML feature reported 1 for a host with no fingerprint. The read layer normalised `-` only. Fixed in BOTH places: tail_zeek_log now normalises both sentinels (the guarantee a mapper cannot bypass -- 79 raw rec.get reads remain across mappers) and the SSL mapper routes its fields through zeek_value. Also found while fixing: tests/test_ja4_fingerprint_integrity.py passed over the live defect.

findings.title: Zeek rotation re-ingests every rotated file in full: tail state is keyed by filename, and the rotated file IS the already-read live file renamed
findings.note: See F011/F019. The rotation NAMING was already fixed (<type>.<timestamp>.log, verified against Zeek's Log::default_rotation_date_format; the old code globbed conn.1.log which Zeek never produces). Rotated files are read oldest-first, so re-reading them is chronological and idempotent.

findings.title: The initial admin password is written to pod logs, and the least-privileged Role can read pod logs
findings.note: Verified with kubectl auth can-i against the live cluster: viewer get pods/log -> YES, viewer get configmaps -> NO, operator create/patch configmaps -> YES. The bootstrap admin password was logged at WARNING, so a READ-ONLY account could recover an ADMIN credential. Exposure was bounded (must_change=True, window ends at first sign-in) but it is a privilege escalation of any duration. FIXED: the password now goes to the weirvern-bootstrap ConfigMap, whose audience is exactly the accounts that can already change the deployment; the log says WHERE rather than what. The write is VERIFIED by reading the value back (this failure would otherwise leave an operator with no credential and no error), the payload is piped on stdin so the value never reaches argv (/proc would expose it), and a cluster-less deployment falls back to the log WITH a note that the channel is weaker. install.sh reads the ConfigMap first and the log second, so deployments predating this change still work. 12 tests, mutation-tested 4 ways -- including one that caught my own source-scanning test surviving removal of the actual read-back comparison, which is why the read-back now has a behavioural test that drives it with a wrong value.

findings.title: Bearer-token auth over cleartext HTTP, on a platform whose purpose is sniffing the LAN
findings.note: The absence of TLS is a DELIBERATE, DOCUMENTED boundary, not a defect: gui_auth.py's threat model has said for some time that it does not defend against 'a network attacker who can terminate TLS (there is no TLS here -- the Service is plain HTTP on a NodePort)'. It defends against another LAN host reaching the port and token guessing, and says so. VERIFIED live: HTTP/1.0 with no TLS on the NodePort. The gap was that this was documented only where DEVELOPERS look -- SECURITY.md never mentioned it. Added there with runnable mitigations (kubectl port-forward svc/weirvern-gui 8088:8088, ssh -L 8088:localhost:8088), BOTH VERIFIED against the live cluster (port-forward returned HTTP 200 {"ok": true}; nodePort 30088 returned 200), now pinned by tests.

findings.title: Teardown of the policy rule is fire-and-forget: a failed removal is indistinguishable from success, and "restored" is asserted from the exit code alone
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed. `remove_forwarding_path` ran five `ip` commands and discarded every return code, returning nothing, so a teardown that removed NOTHING was indistinguishable from one that removed everything. Measured by making all commands fail with 'RTNETLINK answers: Operation not permitted' (what a node without CAP_NET_ADMIN produces): return value None, 4 commands attempted, caller blind. The consequence is not cosmetic -- a leftover rule sends matching traffic to policy table 100, which with the address withdrawn has NO ROUTES, so the rule DROPS that traffic; the operator sees a clean stop and a segment that quietly lost connectivity. FIXED: the function returns the failures and intercept.stop() logs them with the recovery commands. A failure caused by ABSENCE (no such file/process/device) is filtered out, because `ip rule del` fails when the rule is already gone and that is the normal case for a repeated stop -- a warning that is usually wrong is one an operator stops reading. All steps are still attempted (a failing rule deletion must not skip the route flush). NOTE: the report body is not recoverable (tmp/kr2.md was cleaned); this verdict verifies the title's claim directly by running the code.

findings.title: A partial setup failure leaves the policy rule installed over an empty table — the documented black-hole — and `__exit__` provably does not run
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed. `ensure_forwarding_path` appended a problem when the route add failed and then INSTALLED THE POLICY RULE ANYWAY. Measured by failing only the route add (gateway MAC resolving, so the earlier guard did not fire): 'could not add the policy route: RTNETLINK answers: Network is unreachable' AND the rule WAS installed. That is the same black-hole the module's own docstrings describe, created by the FAILURE path: a rule selecting an empty table drops the traffic it matches. The caller then raised InterceptError without removing what had just been installed, and the sysctls from step 0 were left relaxed -- so a REFUSED intercept left the node's ingress policy broken. FIXED IN TWO PLACES: (1) the route failure now short-circuits before the rule is installed, because an absent route alone changes nothing while a rule pointing at an empty table drops traffic; (2) intercept.start()'s refusal path now withdraws the path and restores the sysctls BEFORE raising, and names any cleanup that itself failed in the error message. The refusal still raises -- an intercept that silently did not arm is worse than one that errors. NOTE: the report body is not recoverable (tmp/kr2.md was cleaned); this verdict verifies the title's claim directly by running the code.

findings.title: The management-interface never-intercept rule is prose-only, and the `ZEEK_IFACE` fallback turns a known loch misconfiguration into the siphon poison interface
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed. The 'never intercept the management interface' rule was PROSE on the path that arms an intercept. Measured: ZERO references to MGMT_IFACE in intercept.py, siphon_supervisor.py or worker.py -- `grep -c` returns 0 for all three -- and an InterceptPlan for the management interface constructed and ARMED without objection. The two places that did check are both WRITE-TIME and both bypassable: cli.py when a mode is enabled (and that command takes --force) and cluster_config.validate when a ConfigMap is written (anyone with cluster access can edit a ConfigMap). The consequence in siphon mode is not 'the sensor goes dark' but 'the sensor goes dark WHILE HOLDING the segment's traffic', because the relay is also what keeps the segment reachable. FIXED at the point of no return: Intercept.start() now refuses when MGMT_IFACE equals the intercept interface, BEFORE the sysctls are recorded and before anything is installed, with an explicit `allow_management_iface=False` escape hatch for single-NIC test hosts. VERIFIED in isolation (all later stages stubbed): MGMT_IFACE unset -> armed; MGMT_IFACE==iface -> REFUSED naming the interface and the alternative; different interface -> armed; hatch -> armed. 4 mutations caught including removing the gate and defaulting the hatch to True. The ZEEK_IFACE fallback half was checked too: an unset ZEEK_IFACE resolves to empty, NOT to MGMT_IFACE, so the product does not construct the collision its own gate refuses.

findings.title: In the deployed (read-only) case, every intercept stop logs "could NOT restore … Set them back by hand" and prints a remedy that re-applies the intercept's values
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed. In the deployed container /proc/sys is READ-ONLY, so `SysctlGuard.apply()` correctly writes nothing and records the originals -- but it also marks EVERY managed name `unrestorable`, which `restore()` returns. Measured with can_write=False: applied=[], unrestorable=5 entries, restore() returned 5 names. `intercept.stop()` therefore logged 'could NOT restore 5 network sysctl(s) ... Set them back by hand' on EVERY stop, in the deployment where that is the NORMAL state. The warning was false: this process changed none of those values, and the overlay's privileged init container owns them. This is the same reasoning apply() already applies to per-sysctl write failures ('reporting five per-sysctl write failures on every run trains the reader to ignore them -- and then the one that matters is ignored too'), and needs_node_restore() already existed to describe this case. FIXED: a new `changed_by_us()` separates 'we wrote this and cannot put it back' (WARNING, with the node_restore_command printed) from 'we could not write this at all' (debug, once), so the warning now fires only when it is true. 3 mutations caught, including suppressing the warning unconditionally and dropping the way back. NOTE: report body not recoverable (tmp/kr2.md cleaned); the title's claim was verified directly by running the code. HONEST NOTE ON THE LIVE EVIDENCE: the spurious warning was NOT found in the deployment's retained logs (0 occurrences in 3000 lines), because the cluster runs SENSOR_MODE=loch, which starts no intercept -- and the warning is on the intercept's STOP path, so it needs an intercept to have run and ended. What IS verified live is the condition that triggers it: /proc/sys is genuinely read-only in the worker container ('touch /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/rp_filter' -> Permission denied), and the pre-fix code shape returns 5 names from restore() with applied=[] when run directly. So the defect is real and reproduced, but it becomes visible in production only once siphon mode is used and an intercept is stopped -- which is exactly when an operator would most need to trust the warning.

findings.title: A refused survey is *returned* as `{'ok': False}` after a docstring that promises every failure raises `SonarError`
findings.note: REFUTED, verified by running the function the docstring describes. `sonar.survey()`'s docstring says 'Raises SonarError with a named remedy for every structural refusal', and it does: an unreadable MAC raised SonarError('cannot read a MAC for ...; the survey needs the interface'), and an unobservable interface with no address raised SonarError('no observation'). The {'ok': False} shape the finding describes lives in the HTTP HANDLER (web.py's sonar route, 'except sonar_mod.SonarError as exc: return self._json({"ok": False, "error": str(exc)}, 502)'), which is a DIFFERENT LAYER converting the raise into a response -- correct layering, not a contradiction. Grep confirms sonar.py contains zero occurrences of ok:False (2 ok:True) and 11 SonarError raises. The result that DOES return ok:True without sweeping, `_passive_only_result`, is deliberate and documented: the observation is a genuine answer to 'what network is this', while 'who is alive' is explicitly left unanswered via `swept: None` rather than a fabricated zero.

findings.title: `observe()`'s three measurement fields have no column to land in — computed, None-guarded, then discarded
findings.note: REFUTED, verified against the schema AND the live cluster. The finding claims observe()'s three measurement fields 'have no column to land in'. They do. Migration 007_sensor_capture.sql adds all three explicitly: capture_loss_pct Nullable(Float32), packets_recv Nullable(UInt64), packets_dropped Nullable(UInt64). The write path carries them end to end: sensorwatch.observe() produces them; worker.py's heartbeat passes the whole dict to status.heartbeat(**fields); that function declares all three as keyword parameters, inserts them, and lists them in column_names; status.py reads them back for the UI and the Weirlings view. CONFIRMED LIVE: `DESCRIBE weirvern.sensor_status` returns all three columns, and a live heartbeat within the last 10 minutes holds actual values (capture_loss_pct=0, packets_recv=0, packets_dropped=0). The finding appears to be stale, written against a schema state that the 007 migration had already superseded.

findings.title: The detection → alert path has no test at all (highest-risk untested path)
findings.note: CONFIRMED and addressed with a new test module (tests/test_alert_pipeline.py, 17 tests). `push_alert` was referenced by exactly ONE test, which calls `format_message` to pin a crash that had ALREADY happened in production; nothing exercised push_alert itself, the suppression rules that decide whether an operator is told at all, the audit row every decision should leave, or the failure paths. Structurally the reason is that detection has scores and models to assert on while alerting either fires or does not -- and a defect here produces a SILENCE, which looks exactly like a quiet network. COVERAGE NOW: delivery, the operator payload carrying the reason it fired, log-only mode not claiming a send, per-host cooldown and hourly cap (and that a suppressed alert still leaves an audit row), a Pushover 4xx and an unreachable host both recorded as errors rather than sends, a failed delivery NOT starting the cooldown or consuming the cap, and the audit insert failing without taking the alert. Seven mutations caught. TWO REAL PROBLEMS THE TESTS SURFACED IN MY OWN WORK: (1) one test called the LIVE Pushover API, because it did not request the HTTP stub -- Pushover's own 400 response appears in the captured log, so a unit test sent real HTTP traffic to a third party. The HTTP stub is now autouse and refuses the network unless a test opts in. (2) the first cooldown test used two fixtures that patch the same function, so its 'successful' send actually failed and it asserted against the wrong state. Also: mutation testing found a genuine coverage gap -- the transport-failure branch could start the cooldown with every test still green, because the assertion only covered the HTTP-status path. Both are now pinned. NOTE: the report body is not recoverable (tmp/k12_testing.md was cleaned), so this verdict verifies the title's claim directly against the code.

findings.title: The root-container tripwire cannot see implicit root
findings.note: CONFIRMED with a concrete instance, not a hypothesis. The tripwire resolves `uid = sc.get('runAsUser', pod_sc.get('runAsUser'))` and flags `uid == 0`, so a container that sets runAsUser NOWHERE resolves to None and is skipped -- while a container with neither runAsUser nor runAsNonRoot runs as whatever its IMAGE declares, root by default. MEASURED ON THE LIVE CLUSTER: `goflow2` was exactly that shape (runAsUser and runAsNonRoot unset at both container and pod level) and ran as uid 100 ONLY because the goflow2 image declares `USER flow`. Nothing in the deployment said so; one image update would have collected flow data as root and no guard would have seen the container at all. FIXED IN TWO PLACES: k8s/31-goflow2.yaml sets runAsNonRoot: true and an explicit runAsUser: 100 (runAsNonRoot is load-bearing -- the kubelet ENFORCES it and refuses to start if the image would be root, turning silent drift into a startup failure); and the tripwire now treats an unspecified uid as needing the same deliberate decision as root, with `expected_unspecified` empty so a new uid-less container fails with an explanatory message. VERIFIED LIVE: after apply, the pod spec reads runAsUser=100 runAsNonRoot=true, `id` still returns uid=100(flow), and goflow2 is still collecting (starting collection on 2055 and 6343). VERIFIED BOTH DIRECTIONS IN TESTS: reverting the pin is CAUGHT, and the old resolution over the same manifests returns only zeek and fix-permissions, reproducing the blind spot. NOTE: report body not recoverable (tmp/k9_k8s.md cleaned); this verifies the title's claim against the code and the live pod.

findings.title: A detector that fails to train is silently absent from the ensemble, and its absence *loosens* the agreement gate
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY MEASURING IT, then fixed. `model_agreement = len(detected_by) / active` where `active` counted only detectors reporting `is_ready()`. Since is_ready() means 'trained successfully', a detector that FAILED TO TRAIN removed itself from the DENOMINATOR -- and agreement is a ratio, so losing detectors made it LARGER. MEASURED by driving the real ensemble with the same flow and the same scores, varying only readiness (score 0.550 = the strict tier where min_agreement is the full 0.33): all 4 ready -> agreement 0.25 -> SUPPRESSED; DBSCAN failed -> 0.33 -> ALERT; GB+DBSCAN failed -> 0.50 -> ALERT; only IF ready -> 1.00 -> ALERT with confidence 0.550. A broken model turned a window the ensemble had DELIBERATELY SUPPRESSED into an alert, and the alert looked BETTER corroborated than a healthy one, because confidence is score*agreement: the fewer detectors that worked, the higher the reported confidence. Silent in the worst direction -- it manufactures alerts and its alerts look more certain than real ones. FIXED: the denominator is the ENSEMBLE, not the survivors (`build_detectors` always constructs four, so '3 of 4 agreed' is what a reader expects; a detector that did not train is a detector that did not agree). max(1, ...) keeps the ratio defined. The same spelling appeared in the NEAR-MISS branch and was fixed there too -- found independently by mutation testing, because the first test only covered 1-of-4 where both spellings agree. TWO OF MY OWN ASSERTIONS WERE WRONG FIRST: I asserted the broken case would report LOWER confidence and it reported the SAME (0.675), which is the fix working since the denominator is the ensemble either way; and my first denominator test used scores (0.55) that fused high enough to ALERT instead of producing the near-miss row it read, so it proved nothing until the scores were lowered into the near-miss band. 6 tests, 6 mutations caught. VERIFIED LIVE: fix present in the running image, worker warm-started with all four detectors, live model_agreement values 1.00/0.75/0.50/0.25 (all multiples of 1/4). HONEST LIMIT: the live cluster has no failed detector right now, so production cannot discriminate the fix from the defect; the unit tests and mutations establish it.

findings.title: T1558 "Kerberoasting signature" fires on a raw count of TGS requests — the measurement the comment and the constant name promise is never taken
The rolling `now − interval` query silently skips every window older than one interval — a slow cycle (the 6-hourly retrain) leaves an unlogged blind spot
findings.note: CONFIRMED ON THE LIVE CLUSTER, then fixed. `detection_sweep` computed `since = now() - (AGG_BUCKET_S + detect_interval_s)` EVERY cycle, which is correct only if the previous cycle ran `detect_interval_s` ago. MEASURED from `baseline_history.computed_at` gaps over 48h: 292 cycles, median 300s, p99 966s, MAX 1183s, with ten separate gaps over 600s (1183, 1170, 1138, 949, 897, 893, 847, 835, 818, 778). A 1183s gap means 2 whole 5-minute buckets were never examined -- and the only trace was a heartbeat gap. The cause is in the worker's own loop: `train_if_due` runs BEFORE the sweep and blocks, so the 6-hourly full retrain pushes the next sweep's `now()` forward with `since` moving in lockstep; the loop then compensates the SLEEP at the end, so the cadence looks healthy while the skipped window is never recovered. Those buckets age out of the LOOKBACK, not out of the table, so the data was there and simply stopped being examined. FIXED by carrying the time the sweep STARTED in a checkpoint beside the model artifacts (MODEL_DIR persists across restarts, and a restart was one of the ways the gap occurred) and backing off one bucket: `since = min(now - lookback, cursor - AGG_BUCKET_S)`. The min() keeps the healthy case BIT-IDENTICAL to the old window, which is the property to want in a recovery mechanism, and the back-off re-covers the bucket that was in flight when the previous sweep started. Clamped to retrain_window_h, because a long outage must not become a scoring burst over the whole retention; a gap beyond it is LOGGED as unrecoverable. A future-dated cursor (an NTP step) falls back to the default window with a warning rather than wedging detection forever. The cursor is written only at the END of a completed sweep -- writing it first would turn any mid-sweep exception into a permanently skipped window. 10 tests, 9 mutations caught: the first mutation run MISSED 'never record coverage at all' because my tests only proved the empty case does not advance, never that a completed sweep does; that test was added and the mutation now bites.

findings.title: All weight settings — including `weight_baseline_missing` — are inert under the default max fusion: an operator's validated edit changes nothing
One raising sub-query collapses the whole Health view and misreports the cause as "cannot reach ClickHouse"
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed. Six probes in `collect_health` were wrapped in `if err is None:` with NO else branch, so a sub-query that raised removed that probe's ROW from the report entirely. MEASURED by driving the real collect_health with a stub failing exactly one query: `tables` raising -> 5 probes with ingest_freshness/alerts_24h/fingerprint_feed MISSING; `detect_loop` raising -> 6 probes with detect_loop MISSING. A consumer cannot tell 'this check passed' from 'this check never ran', and the failure is attributed nowhere because every remaining row reads normally. Same class as F081 and F024. FIXED with a `_probe_failed` helper that emits the row with ok=False and carries the underlying exception; ok=False rather than the tri-state None, because a probe that cannot run is not a pass whereas None means 'measured and not applicable'. TWO MORE SHAPES FOUND IN THE SAME PROBE: (a) alerts_24h unpacked r[0]/r[1] for every row, so a row with fewer than 2 elements raised IndexError STRAIGHT OUT of collect_health, taking out the entire view and blaming this probe for a shape problem from the query result -- a malformed row is now reported as malformed; (b) zeek_freshness had a branch that fell through and added NO row (records present with a NULL age matched neither the empty case nor the age-present case) -- the same absence F081 fixed one branch up, left in place. A FOURTH PROBLEM WAS IN MY OWN CODE: my new fingerprint_feed probe read frows[0][1] directly and would have crashed the whole report on a one-element row -- the exact shape the first fix was about -- surviving the live deployment only because ClickHouse always returns both columns; testing against SHAPES rather than only a live server is what caught it. One existing test asserted the OLD contract (`detect_loop not in names`) and was inverted deliberately: the intent was right, the mechanism (silence) was unreadable. 7 tests, 7 mutations caught. VERIFIED LIVE: 8 of 8 probes present, none truncated.

findings.title: Auto-refresh reloads only the Health view, whatever tab is visible
A signed-in viewer holding the operator token is refused as a viewer — the token is silently ignored
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY DRIVING THE REAL HANDLER, then fixed. `_authorize` returned the SESSION's verdict first, so a request carrying a viewer session AND the valid operator token was refused as a viewer with the token never examined; `_caller_role` had the same shape. MEASURED: viewer session + VALID token -> 403 'this account is a viewer' (via=session); no session + VALID token -> AUTHORIZED (via=token). The SAME credential was accepted or refused depending only on whether the caller happened to be signed in as a viewer. NOTHING WAS PROTECTED BY THE ORDERING: a viewer holding the token can present it with no session and be authorised, which is the second line. What it cost was the operator's ability to use their break-glass credential from a signed-in browser, plus a refusal saying 'ask an admin' when the needed credential was already on the request. Both docstrings already promised the token was admin-equivalent and 'works everywhere an admin does'; the code did not implement it. FIXED so the token wins where both are present, with via='token' keeping the write attributable to the credential that opened the gate; a viewer WITHOUT the token still gets the viewer refusal. The token check is gated=True so a wrong token still counts toward the escalating delay, and the passive _token_role() still passes no client so a read cannot meter someone else's address. 7 mutations caught. ONE WAS MISSED first (dropping gated=True) because my stub's delay_for only recorded the address: what the mutation breaks is the COUNTING, so the replacement test asserts the failure count directly. VERIFIED LIVE for the token paths (valid token reaches the route, wrong token 401, no credentials 401). NOT VERIFIED LIVE for the viewer-session case: my out-of-band viewer account went to the wrong ConfigMap (ClusterConfig defaults to weirvern-env; the store's real client is bound to weirvern-users -- correct at its call site), so sign-in failed and the account was never visible to the GUI. My error, cleaned up; that case rests on the handler-level tests, which call the same _authorize the HTTP route calls.

`.log.json` "support" reads JSON logs through a TSV parser and silently ingests nothing
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed. `tail_zeek_dir` has always listed BOTH `conn.log` and `conn.log.json` as supported filenames -- it looks for the pair explicitly -- but `tail_zeek_log` read every line as TSV. A Zeek JSON log has NO `#` header, so `fields` stayed empty and every line hit the 'data before header' branch: read, discarded, and the cursor advanced past it. MEASURED with a real two-row conn.log.json: inserted 0 of 2, cursor advanced 832 of 832, no header found. So an operator who switched Zeek to JSON output got EMPTY TABLES, no error, and a warning repeating once per line -- the supported-filename list and the parser disagreed, which is the shape this campaign keeps finding. FIXED by parsing JSON lines when the filename ends .log.json (the same signal the caller keys on, and it cannot be confused by a record's content), with a `_json_field_value` normaliser so the mappers see ONE input contract instead of two: null -> absent, booleans -> T/F (exactly Zeek's own TSV convention), lists -> comma-joined (Zeek's set separator), numbers -> their string form. VERIFIED: a JSON log ingests 2 of 2, and THE SAME RECORD read as JSON and as TSV produces IDENTICAL values on every one of the 15 columns. A malformed JSON line is REPORTED and skipped with the cursor still advancing, and a TSV file misnamed .log.json is refused visibly rather than silently ingesting nothing. 15 tests in the module, 6 mutations caught including reverting to TSV-for-everything, detecting JSON from content, letting a null through, rendering a boolean as 'True', and swallowing a malformed line at debug. LATENT IN THIS DEPLOYMENT: the live sensor writes Zeek's default TSV output, and `find` returns no *.log.json anywhere, so nothing here was losing data -- it would have bitten on switching Zeek to JSON. MY OWN TEST ERROR: the malformed-line test used a client that REJECTS single rows, so the one valid row was rejected by the stub and the count was 0 for a reason unrelated to JSON; the fixture accepts now.

zeek_freshness probe is silently absent when the sensor has never produced a row
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed -- same class as F022/F024 in this campaign. The zeek_freshness probe was added to the report ONLY when a freshness age came back, so an empty zeek_conn produced NO row at all. MEASURED with an empty table: probes were ['clickhouse','tables','ingest_freshness','models','detect_loop','alerts_24h'] and zeek_freshness was ABSENT. The sibling `ingest_freshness` two probes above already reports its own empty case as a FAILURE with a remedy, so the two disagreed about emptiness. THE FIX NEEDED A THIRD STATE, not a boolean: the comment above the probe said 'only meaningful if the sensor is enabled' and that was NEVER IMPLEMENTED -- collect_health has no way to know a sensor is deployed, so the old code used 'data exists' as a proxy and collapsed two different facts into one outcome. So Probe.ok became bool|None; None is NOT APPLICABLE, decided on EVIDENCE (a sensor_status heartbeat in the last 24h) rather than on absence being interpreted; HealthReport.ok excludes Nones so a not-applicable row can neither mask a real failure nor invent one. THE GUI HAD THE SAME BUG and would have undone the fix: `checks.filter((c) => !c.ok)` counts null as failing and `c.ok ? 'ok' : 'FAIL'` paints it red, so the probe added to stop silence reading as health would have read as a FAILURE. Fixed in soc.js: n/a rows are excluded from the counts and rendered as 'n/a', with the summary and pill stating how many were not applicable. `ip rule del priority 1000` can delete a foreign routing rule, silently
findings.note: CONFIRMED ON A REAL KERNEL, then fixed -- and the fix took two attempts, the second corrected by mutation testing. `remove_forwarding_path` deleted `priority 1000` UNCONDITIONALLY, assuming the priority was ours. The TABLE number (100) is ours; the priority is just a number and 1000 is round enough that other software uses it. MEASURED: planted a foreign rule `1000: from all lookup 200`, ran the teardown, and the rule was DELETED while the function returned [] -- reporting no failures. Silent damage to another tool's policy routing, from a function whose job is to clean up after itself. The table-scoped sweep in the same function was already careful about this; the unconditional line ran FIRST. FIRST FIX (guarded the deletion with a selector check) WAS REDUNDANT, which mutation testing caught: with the guard returning False, the sweep still issued `ip rule del priority 1000` for our rule, because the sweep derives priorities from `_policy_rule_priorities()` which is already table-scoped. The two lines were the SAME command reached two ways, so no test could distinguish them and removing the priority path entirely left the suite green. FINAL FIX: the unconditional line is DELETED, not guarded, leaving the table-scoped sweep as the single priority-based deletion -- strictly safer (it can only match a rule selecting OUR table) and strictly more complete (every such priority, not just POLICY_PRIORITY). The guard helper was removed with it, since dead code is one more thing to reason about. VERIFIED ON THE REAL KERNEL with both rules planted at once: priority 1000 (foreign, table 200) SURVIVED, and priority 1001 (ours, table 100 -- a priority the OLD code would never have touched) was REMOVED. 15 tests in the module, 3 mutations caught including reinstating the unconditional delete, dropping the table filter, and sweeping only our fixed priority.

findings.title: Never-intercept roles are unenforced for whole-segment intercepts (`--all` / `*`)
findings.note: CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT, then fixed -- the same class as F033, in the neighbouring path. `never_intercept_hits` derives the roles a target must never hold (the resolver the sensor uses, its management address, the Kubernetes API server) from KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST, MGMT_ADDR and /etc/resolv.conf, and was consulted ONLY under `if only:` -- the named-host path. The whole-segment path skipped just {our_ip, gateway_ip}, so every other derivable role stayed a candidate. MEASURED on a /24 containing them: the K8s API server (.55) and the sensor's management address (.44) both landed in plan.hosts, with 252 hosts planned. So the SAFER-LOOKING path -- a whole segment, no explicit names -- was the one that could forge the mapping for the control plane the sensor reports to while it relays, which is precisely the failure this check exists to prevent and does not degrade gracefully: the sensor loses its own path exactly when it is holding the segment's traffic. FIXED: the derivable roles are excluded from a whole-segment build BEFORE the candidate list is formed, so they are not even ARP-swept (a sweep toward the control plane is traffic the sensor should not be generating either), and each exclusion is logged with its role. The path deliberately DIFFERS from the named one: a whole-segment build cannot REFUSE, because refusing would make the feature impossible on any segment containing a nameserver or API server, which is every real segment -- so it excludes and reports, while the named path still refuses and still honours --force-unsafe. VERIFIED after the fix: .55 and .44 gone from the plan, 250 hosts planned, 251 probed (both down by exactly 2), ordinary hosts still included, named path still REFUSES, force_unsafe still overrides a non-structural role, structural roles impossible regardless. 9 tests, 4 mutations caught. MY OWN PROBE ERROR, worth recording: an earlier check reported the named path as 'RETURNED (should refuse)' because build_plan LOGS the refusal and returns None rather than raising, and my probe only caught exceptions -- a false alarm about a regression I had not caused. The tests now assert on the None directly.

Partial per-block aggregates blinded T1046/T1018: every discovery threshold counted one insert block, not the window
findings.note: CONFIRMED ON THE LIVE CLUSTER, then fixed. A ClickHouse materialized view fires PER INSERT BLOCK, so every insert into weirvern.flows writes its own aggregate row for the same (window_start, src_addr); the target tables are MergeTree(), not ReplacingMergeTree, so those partial rows are NEVER merged. MEASURED over 24h: flows_aggregated 592 host-windows with 555 fragmented (93.8%), worst case 46 rows; flows_aggregated_diversity 589/552 (93.7%), also 46 worst case. One worst-case window's 46 partial rows held unique_dst_ports of [1,1,1,2,1,1,...2]: the sweep saw (max) 2 ports while the window held (sum) 81. TWO failures compounded: `flows` was one dict PER PARTIAL ROW (up to 46 scorer inputs for one host-window), and `flow_by_key`'s plain dict assignment meant the LAST partial won -- typically the smallest block, so T1046's port threshold was evaluated against the least informative row of the window. A 500-port scan spread over 46 insert blocks read as 1-2 ports, below every discovery threshold. FIXED by folding partials into ONE row per host-window before scoring: additive columns summed, cardinalities RE-DERIVED FROM THE RAW FLOW TABLE (summing partials is an upper bound, and an inflated count that gates a scan rule manufactures false positives -- trading a gap for false positives is not a fix). A THIRD, DEEPER CASE WAS FOUND BY MEASURING RATHER THAN REASONING: port_entropy is a per-block measurement that CANNOT be recovered by folding at all -- entropy over 2 ports is bounded by log2(2)=1.0 however many blocks are added, while T1046 requires 3.0. Live per-block entropy on fragmented windows measured 0 to 0.54. So entropy, stddev and active_minutes are RECOMPUTED from raw flows using the materialized view's own expressions, including its `dst_port > 0` filter so both paths describe the same population. The raw-read failure path falls back to summing and LOGS that the counts are an upper bound, because a silently approximate threshold is how this hid. VERIFIED against the real code on the deployed cluster with a synthetic 300-port scan arriving in 60 small blocks: the old path mapped NOTHING (5 ports seen), the fixed path maps T1046 + T1595 + T1018 with the evidence reading '300 distinct destination ports (threshold 100), port entropy 7.90 (threshold 3.0)'. Live sweeps show 0 fallback warnings, so cardinalities are exact. 11 tests, 7 mutations caught -- including two that were MISSED first (deleting entropy from the SELECT, and dropping the dst_port > 0 filter) because every other test replaces db.fetch_rows_named wholesale and never examines the SQL the product issues; a query-text test now pins those.

findings.title: Train and score encoded the day of week on different calendars: ClickHouse toDayOfWeek (Mon=1) vs Python weekday() (Mon=0)
findings.note: CONFIRMED AGAINST CLICKHOUSE ITSELF, then fixed and deployed. This is the '7-feature train/score scale mismatch' recorded as an open high-severity item. The training queries in models/detectors.py encode the day of week with ClickHouse's `toDayOfWeek`, which is Monday=1 through Sunday=7; `features.extract_features` encoded the SAME window with Python's `datetime.weekday()`, which is Monday=0 through Sunday=6 -- a constant off-by-one on the day index. MEASURED against the cluster for a Wednesday window, which both sides agree is index 3 vs 2: from ClickHouse dow_sin 0.43388373911755823 / dow_cos -0.900968867902419; from the module dow_sin 0.9749279121818236 / dow_cos -0.22252093395631434. So the model learned one point on the weekly circle and was asked to score another: the model was not wrong, it was answering a different question. Nothing raised, because the vector had the right LENGTH and every value was a valid number -- the silent class this campaign keeps finding. The `is_business_hours` predicate was CONSISTENT on both sides (ClickHouse `< 6` and Python `< 5` both mean Mon-Fri), so only the cyclic pair was wrong; the fix moves the whole encoding to `isoweekday()` and restates the predicate as `< 6` on the same number the query uses, so the two halves cannot sit on different calendars. FIXED IN features.py; VERIFIED in the running container: 14 of 14 features now agree to 4.44e-16. THE ARTIFACTS NEEDED RETRAINING, and this is the part worth remembering: the persisted IF/GB/DBSCAN pickles were fit at 03:54 on the old encoding, and because scoring uses the LIVE feature list and the artifact's own fitted preprocessor, a corrected encoder plus a stale artifact is STILL mismatched in both directions. The three artifacts were renamed to .premismatch (not deleted, so a rollback is possible) and the worker was restarted; it trained cold at 09:37 (Isolation Forest on 80000 samples, anomaly rate 3.300%). 11 tests, 6 mutations caught -- including two CROSS-FILE mutations changing the training SQL itself, which is the drift this defect was. MY OWN ERROR: my first transcription of ClickHouse's outputs for days 4 and 5 was wrong in the last two digits and the test passed anyway because the tolerance was 1e-9; the values are now quoted verbatim from a live query rather than re-derived in Python, which would have compared the module against the same mistake a second time.

findings.title: Every worker restart re-read all Zeek logs, and for the tables with no dedup key that multiplied model inputs (notice_count 64x)
findings.note: CONFIRMED ON THE LIVE CLUSTER, then fixed. Found while refuting the above. `tail_zeek_dir` kept its per-log cursors in a DICT IN MEMORY (keyed by filename), so every worker restart re-read all Zeek logs from offset zero. The NetFlow tailer got a persisted cursor in F018; this path never did. THE COST WAS NOT STARTUP WORK, which is what the code's own docstring assumed: `zeek_notice` and `zeek_dhcp` are plain `MergeTree` with NO dedup key, because their `uid` is EMPTY -- they cannot be `ReplacingMergeTree ORDER BY (ts, uid)` the way `zeek_conn`/`zeek_dns` are. A re-read therefore ADDS instead of collapsing. MEASURED: zeek_notice held 6556 rows for 162 distinct (ts, note, msg) groups with single rows appearing 64 times; zeek_dhcp 3201 rows for 65 distinct (ts, mac) with rows appearing 47 times. And `zeek_features.py` aggregates those tables with plain count(), so `zeek_notice_count` read 64 where the truth was 1 -- a 64x inflation of a LIVE MODEL INPUT, growing with every restart. FIXED by persisting the cursor per log file, with a dedicated `load_zeek_state`/`save_zeek_state` pair because the Zeek cursor must carry the parsed `#fields` header alongside the offset: a Zeek data line is positional, so an offset restored without its field names maps nothing. The checkpoint reuses the F018 path helper (MODEL_DIR, writable, survives restarts) and inherits its rotation revalidation. VERIFIED: a simulated restart now ingests 0 from an unchanged file (was: everything), still ingests exactly the 2 rows appended while it was down, and a rotation is still caught rather than trusted. 5 tests, 6 mutations caught. A SECOND DEFECT WAS FOUND IN MY OWN FIRST VERSION: I called `save_tail_state` and then patched the header into the same file, but `save_tail_state` writes a FRESH payload and atomically replaces the file, so it wiped the header written a moment earlier and only the ordering decided which keys survived. The payload is now built and written once. MY TEST WAS ALSO WRONG: I asserted the separator with an INVENTED comma-separated Zeek log; real Zeek always writes '#separator \x09' (verified on every log on the sensor), so that fixture described a file that does not exist. LIMITATION, MEASURED AND STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the live deployment has 367 Zeek files but the tailer's `depth=50` bound per type per pass means checkpoints accumulate across passes, so the first restart after this fix still re-read a large set of previously-unechecked rotated files. The fix removes the re-read for everything checkpointed and stops the multiplication going forward; it does not retroactively clean the rows already duplicated, which is left as an operator decision.

findings.title: Host identification had no input for 20 hours and every health probe read green: nothing measured the fingerprint feed
findings.note: CONFIRMED ON THE LIVE CLUSTER, then fixed. `host_fingerprints` is the input to host identification (the raw MAC-vendor/DHCP-hostname/JA4/software observations that `build_identity` classifies). MEASURED: newest observation 72,837s old = 20.2 hours, while EVERY probe on the health page read green. NOTHING in the admin surface reads that table -- `grep -c host_fingerprints weirvern/admin/*.py` returns nothing -- and the probe that looks like it covers this, `identity`, reports COVERAGE from the VERDICT table, which shrinks slowly as hosts age out of a 7-day window, so a dead feed looks like a stable deployment for most of a week. The reported symptom was `_record_observations` logging dropped rows at DEBUG. THAT LOGGING IS CORRECT AND IS NOT THE FIX: identification is enrichment, and losing flow data to report a fingerprint problem would trade the important thing for the useful one. The real defect is the MISSING MEASUREMENT -- if failures are deliberately quiet, something must measure the result, or a total outage and a quiet segment are indistinguishable. FIXED with a `fingerprint_feed` probe on the age of the newest observation, tri-state like zeek_freshness so a NetFlow-only deployment (no Zeek sensor, correctly no observations) reports ok=None with a detail naming both cases. THE THRESHOLD IS MEASURED, NOT PICKED: my first version used 24h on the reasoning that a quiet segment produces nothing for hours, and deploying it at 20h17m of real staleness still reported `ok` -- a bound that only fires after the failure has run most of a day is barely a probe. Measured healthy gaps are median 73s, p90 212s, p99 2,277s, so the bound is 4h: an order of magnitude above p99 and well below the measured stall, with a test pinning it between those two measured values. VERIFIED LIVE: every other probe green, overall ok False, row reads '[FAIL] fingerprint_feed newest observation 20h20m ago (5872 in 7d)'. 4 tests, 6 mutations caught. THE UNDERLYING STALL IS NOT A CODE DEFECT and is recorded as such: each source's newest observation coincides EXACTLY with the newest log file of its type (ja4 13:46 vs ssl.*.log, software 13:24, dhcp 12:48 vs dhcp.*.log), while Zeek rotates dns/conn/stats/notice/capture_loss hourly through today and writes NO rotations for dhcp, ssl or software -- those three analyzers produce nothing on this segment. Two unconfirmed candidates: the capture interface is a veth that may not carry DHCP/TLS broadcast traffic, and the site policy's 'dhcp ALREADY WRITING' comment was true when written.
